title: Desert Climate Overview
description: Mecca has a hot desert climate, classified BWh in the Koppen-Geiger system, set in a valley among mountains in western Saudi Arabia about 70 kilometres from the Red Sea. Summers are long, very hot and almost rainless, winters are warm by most standards, and the city receives strong sunshine for most of the year, with published sunshine totals around 3,387 hours per year. The valley setting shapes local weather: heat builds in the valley, night cooling is limited compared with open desert, and rare rain can run quickly off rock and paved surfaces into low ground. Climate is the background condition for every other record in this pair, because water supply, heat management, air quality and crowd safety in Mecca are all designed around sustained heat and scarce rain, and the crowd-science pair returns to heat as a safety factor. This record states climate in general factual terms; monthly figures are given in the next record with their sources. The demo below converts the published annual sunshine total into an average per day, a simple check that a yearly climate figure is plausible.

title: Rainfall and Temperature (Published Data)
description: Published climate datasets disagree on Mecca's exact averages, so this record states the range and the disagreement. Climate-data.org gives an average annual temperature of 28.6 degrees Celsius with annual rainfall of 130 millimetres, while timeanddate's Makkah table gives a mean temperature near 89 degrees Fahrenheit (about 32 degrees Celsius) with annual precipitation of 3.02 inches (about 77 millimetres), and other published summaries give about 121 millimetres. The honest summary is therefore an average annual temperature in the high twenties to low thirties Celsius, summer daytime highs commonly around 40 to 43 degrees Celsius with July the warmest month, winter daytime highs around 29 degrees Celsius, and annual rainfall roughly 77 to 130 millimetres depending on dataset and period, concentrated in the cooler months from November to January, with June often near zero. No single dataset is silently treated as exact, and no daily forecast is claimed here. The demo below averages the published annual rainfall figures cited and converts between millimetres and inches, so dataset spread is visible.

title: Water Supply History
description: Mecca's water history is a history of carrying water to a valley city with no large local river, for a population that swells seasonally. In early periods water came from wells, springs and cisterns, and from the historic Ain Zubayda aqueduct system associated with the Abbasid period, which brought water from springs toward Mecca along channels. In the modern period the city came to depend on piped supply, storage reservoirs, and, increasingly, desalinated water piped from the Red Sea coast, with groundwater as a smaller part of supply. The old well at the centre of the city, known as Zamzam, remains a religiously significant water source in Islamic tradition; this record notes its traditional significance and its historic role, and treats modern municipal supply volumes as a separate engineering matter. Where a historic volume or date is not verified in the public record consulted, it is not stated. The modern desalination and distribution system is treated in the next record. The demo below compares three supply shares that sum to one hundred percent, showing how a supply mix is checked for completeness.

title: Desalination (General, Published)
description: Desalination is the backbone of modern water supply for Mecca and the wider western Saudi coast, because local rainfall and groundwater cannot meet the demand of a large city plus pilgrimage peaks. Seawater from the Red Sea is treated at large coastal plants, notably in the Jeddah and Yanbu areas and at Shoaiba, and the treated water is piped inland to Mecca and stored in reservoirs for distribution. Saudi Arabia is among the world's largest producers of desalinated water, and published national reporting describes desalination as supplying a majority of municipal water in the Kingdom's coastal cities, though the exact share for Mecca alone is not stated here because a single verified Mecca-only share is not in the public record consulted. Desalination carries energy costs and produces concentrated brine, which is why the conservation and reuse records in this pair matter as much as new supply. This record describes desalination in general published terms and gives no plant-level capacity that is not separately sourced. The demo below estimates treated-water output from seawater intake at a stated recovery rate, the basic desalination arithmetic.

title: Wastewater and Reuse
description: Wastewater in Mecca is collected through the municipal sewer network and treated at treatment plants, with treated water reused for irrigation, landscaping and other non-potable purposes where regulations allow, rather than discharged unused. Reuse matters in a desert city because every cubic metre reused is a cubic metre that desalination does not have to produce, and because irrigation demand for parks, roadside planting and the green spaces in this pair can be met without drawing on drinking-water supply. Saudi national policy has promoted treated-wastewater reuse for irrigation and landscaping, and published reporting describes reuse as a growing share of non-potable supply, though a single verified current reuse volume for Mecca alone is not stated here. Treatment quality, public-health rules and the separation of potable and non-potable networks are the governing constraints, and this record does not claim any reuse for drinking, which would require a separate published basis. Greywater reuse inside buildings is a separate, smaller practice, governed by building rules. The demo below computes reuse volume from wastewater treated at a stated reuse share, the planning arithmetic for an irrigation programme.

title: Flood History and Management (Published Events)
description: Mecca's valley setting makes flash flooding a real, published risk: rare heavy rain on rock and paved ground runs quickly into low streets and valleys, and the city has experienced damaging floods in its history, including widely reported floods in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Published flood-management responses include dams and retention structures in the valleys above the city, drainage channels and culverts through urban areas, early-warning and road-closure procedures during storms, and development controls on the most flood-exposed ground. Because rainfall totals are small on average, flood risk is easy to understate from annual averages alone; it is the intensity of a single storm, not the annual total, that produces a flood, and this record therefore treats storm intensity, not annual rainfall, as the flood variable. Specific historic flood casualty figures and damage totals are not stated here, because this pair reports management and risk in general terms and does not dwell on individual events. Current flood warnings must come from official channels at the time, not from this record. The demo below applies the rational runoff formula, discharge equals runoff coefficient times intensity times area, to a model storm, showing why a paved valley floods faster than open ground.

title: Heat Management and Shade Engineering
description: Heat management in Mecca is a matter of engineering and behaviour together, because summer daytime temperatures commonly reach the low forties Celsius and pilgrimage rites and ordinary life continue outdoors in that heat. Published heat measures include shaded walkways and courtyards, misting and ventilation in crowded areas, air-conditioned indoor spaces and transport, light-coloured and reflective surfaces, planting and water features where water allows, and scheduling that avoids the hottest hours where ritual and work schedules permit. The Grand Mosque area and the holy sites use large-scale shade, cooling and ventilation systems, and health authorities publish heat advice for pilgrims, including hydration, rest and shade, though this record gives no personal medical advice. Shade engineering is judged by the temperature a person actually experiences in shade and moving air, not by the air temperature alone, and the heat-and-crowd record in the companion pair models that interaction. Materials, orientation and wind matter as much as any single device. The demo below models felt temperature as air temperature minus shade benefit minus airflow benefit, a simple illustration of combined cooling, not a physiological model.

title: Air Quality
description: Air quality in Mecca is shaped by desert dust, vehicle emissions, construction dust and, at pilgrimage peaks, very large numbers of vehicles and people in a valley that limits dispersion. Published regional air-quality reporting for Saudi cities commonly tracks particulate matter from dust and combustion, nitrogen dioxide from traffic, and ozone on hot sunny days, and desert dust storms can raise particulate levels sharply for hours or days regardless of local traffic controls. Valley geography matters: calm, hot conditions can trap pollutants near the ground, while wind can clear them quickly, so air quality varies by day and by district, not only by season. Monitoring stations, treated in the monitoring record, give the measured picture, and this record does not state a single air-quality index for the city, because a single number would hide the variation between dust days, traffic peaks and quiet periods. Construction and road works are managed with dust controls in published project reporting. The demo below averages daily particulate readings over a model week and counts days above a stated threshold, the basic form of an air-quality summary.

title: Waste Management
description: Waste management in Mecca must handle ordinary resident waste all year and a very large seasonal surge during Hajj and Ramadan, when millions of visitors produce packaging, food waste and single-use items in a few weeks. Municipal collection scales up with extra crews, containers and transfer capacity, and published Hajj reporting describes large seasonal clean-up operations around the holy sites, with sorting and recycling for some streams and landfill for the remainder. Food waste, plastics and cardboard dominate the pilgrim waste stream, and litter control in crowded areas is a safety matter as well as a cleanliness matter, because waste on walkways and stairs creates slip and trip hazards in dense crowds. Long-term published Saudi waste policy aims to divert more waste from landfill through recycling and treatment, and Mecca's seasonal surge is a test case for that policy. A single verified current waste tonnage for Mecca alone is not stated here, because seasonal totals and resident totals are reported on different bases and must not be added silently. The demo below estimates seasonal waste from visitors, days and kilograms per visitor per day, the planning arithmetic for a clean-up operation.

title: Green Spaces
description: Green spaces in Mecca are limited by desert climate, water scarcity and dense urban land, and they are therefore planned as irrigated parks, planted courtyards, roadside planting and landscaped public spaces rather than as large natural forests. Parks in residential districts, planting around public buildings, and landscaped areas near pilgrimage routes provide shade, rest and a cooler microclimate, and their irrigation is a direct claim on the water system, which is why the reuse record matters to this record. Published city descriptions name parks and landscaped areas in residential districts and around the holy sites, but a single verified total green area per resident is not stated here, because park inventories change with development and are reported on different boundaries. In a desert city, green space is judged by shade, irrigation source and survival through summer, not by area alone, and planting that cannot survive the summer without excessive drinking water is a poor use of scarce supply. Native and drought-tolerant species are preferred in published landscaping practice. The demo below computes green space per resident from a stated park area and population, the standard comparative ratio.

title: Environmental Monitoring
description: Environmental monitoring in Mecca covers weather, air quality, water quality and, during Hajj, crowd and health indicators, through fixed stations, mobile measurements and satellite data, coordinated across municipal, meteorological and health bodies. Weather stations record temperature, humidity, wind and rainfall, air stations record particulates and gases, and water monitoring covers supply quality and treated-wastewater quality for reuse. Published monitoring summaries for Saudi cities describe expanding networks and public reporting, but a single verified current station count for Mecca alone is not stated here, because networks grow and station lists are published by different bodies on different dates. Monitoring matters most when it is timely: a dust warning, a heat warning or a flood warning is useful only if it reaches the people and operators who must act on it before the event, and the monitoring record in the crowd-science pair treats real-time warning as a safety system, not as a data archive. Data quality, calibration and public access are the standing tests of any network.
